true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: list views pass only promRule, allowing the Silence notifications action to appear and toggle showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer requires a Grafana Ruler rule and therefore never renders, leaving the action with no visible effect.

false_positives.candidate:
skipToken does not produce neutral Grafana abilities

useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts skipToken to undefined and still evaluates useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. With an undefined rule, some abilities are not neutral: for example Duplicate can become supported and allowed based on global Grafana create permissions. This can make actions appear in contexts where there is no Grafana rule, such as non-Grafana Prometheus rules or missing promRule data. skipToken should return [false, false] for all requested actions.

Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable

useAllRulerRuleAbilities hard-codes isFederated = false, and the deprecated useAllAlertRuleAbilities wrapper no longer checks the original rule group with isFederatedRuleGroup. Previously, federated rules were considered immutable and update/delete/duplicate actions were hidden. After this change, federated rules may be shown as editable or deletable in the UI, which is a permission/contract regression unless federation support is intentionally being removed.

Delete is not rendered for Grafana Prometheus-only rules even when allowed

canDelete is computed from either ruler abilities or Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the Delete menu item is only rendered when canDelete && rulerRule. In the ruler-less alert list view rulerRule is undefined, so users with delete permission will never see Delete for Grafana rules. If deletion is intended to remain available after removing ruler fetches, this condition needs to support Prometheus-only rules.

Grafana rule key contains an extra closing brace

getGrafanaRuleKey returns a string ending with an extra '}' after rule.uid. The key is currently not used in the Grafana branch because the key prop is missing, but the malformed key will be confusing if reused later.

Clipboard copy promise has no rejection handler

navigator.clipboard?.writeText(text).then(...) does not handle promise rejection. If clipboard access is denied or fails, the app can produce an unhandled promise rejection and the user receives no feedback. A catch handler should be added.

Inline action arrays defeat memoization in ability hooks

AlertRuleMenu passes new array literals to useRulerRuleAbilities and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities on every render. Those hooks memoize their result based on the actions array reference, so the mapped abilities are recomputed on every render for every row. Extracting the action list to a stable constant would avoid unnecessary work in large rule lists.

runSplitQuery re-interpolates already interpolated shard-split queries

runSplitQuery now unconditionally applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to every target. It is also called from shardQuerySplitting.ts after runShardSplitQuery has already applied template variables and after interpolateShardingSelector has rewritten the expression. This causes template replacement to run twice on the same query. Template replacement is not generally idempotent: dollar signs introduced by variable values or by the first interpolation can be treated as variables on the second pass, corrupting the LogQL expression or silently dropping text. It can also reapply variable/filter substitution multiple times. Consider an internal non-interpolating split path or a flag to skip interpolation when targets are already interpolated.

$__range splitting guard is evaluated after interpolation

querySupportsSplitting relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr), and the comment says queries using $__range must not be split. Because the targets are now passed through applyTemplateVariables before this check, any $__range or ${__range} macro that is replaced will no longer be present in expr, so the query will be classified as splittable. This can split queries that were explicitly meant to be excluded and produce incorrect range vectors or results. The exclusion should be based on the raw query expression, or range macros must be preserved until after the check.

Queries that interpolate to empty are no longer filtered out

runShardSplitQuery filters query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables, whereas the previous implementation interpolated first and then filtered. If a target has an expression such as a template variable that resolves to an empty string, it now passes the filter, is grouped/sharded, and can be sent to Loki as an empty query. The same missing post-interpolation filter exists in querySplitting.ts. Filter hidden/empty queries again after interpolation.

Missing interpolation edge-case tests for $__range and empty results

The new interpolation tests only cover $__auto and $step. They do not verify that queries containing $__range remain excluded from splitting after interpolation, nor that queries whose expression interpolates to an empty string are skipped. These are the edge cases made more fragile by moving interpolation to the start of the splitting pipeline.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice performs a separate COUNT(*) to check the active-device limit and then runs the upsert in another session without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from distinct new device IDs can both observe count < device_limit and then insert, exceeding the configured limit. If device_limit is intended as a hard bound, enforce it atomically (for example with a conditional insert/update, transactional locking, or a database constraint/trigger).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both recommend atomic enforcement through transactions or locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Failed device-limit writes are cached, allowing the limit to be bypassed

tagDeviceUI stores the device ID in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice propagates the error and the first anonymous authentication fails, but the cache entry remains. For the cache TTL (29 minutes), subsequent requests with the same device ID return nil from tagDeviceUI without checking the limit or persisting the device, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. This allows a device rejected by the limit to access anonymously and makes the limit ineffective. Cache only after successful persistence or delete the cache entry on error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice, leaves it cached when ErrDeviceLimitReached occurs, and allows subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for the 29-minute cache TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
COUNT query is executed in the authentication path when the limit is enabled

When device_limit is greater than zero, every anonymous request that misses the local cache runs COUNT(*) over anon_device during authentication before upserting. On instances with many anonymous devices, this can add latency and database load. Consider a cheaper enforcement strategy, such as an approximate cached counter or a conditional write that avoids a separate count query.

No tests cover device-limit failures through TagDevice/authentication

The added store test checks that a second device is rejected when the limit is 1, but there is no service-level test for TagDevice with a configured AnonymousDeviceLimit. In particular, nothing verifies that a limit-reached error blocks anonymous authentication and that a failed write is not cached, which is the interaction that allows the limit to be bypassed. Add integration tests with a non-zero device limit and repeated requests for the same device ID.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsynchronized initialization/read of @loaded_locales

`ensure_loaded!` initializes and checks `@loaded_locales` outside `LOAD_MUTEX`, while `load_locale` mutates the same array inside the mutex. Under multithreaded servers this can race, causing duplicate loads or lost/cleared loaded-locale state. Initialize the array in a thread-safe way and perform the check under the same mutex.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same concurrency issue: @loaded_locales is lazily initialized and accessed without synchronization. The candidate adds details about mutex coverage and potential race effects, consistent with the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests

The accelerator loads translation data lazily, and `translate` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`. The new fallback locales are loaded only by `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, which is invoked solely from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any server-side translation outside that controller path (background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, `I18n.with_locale` blocks, or errors before the filter) will not have the fallback locale YAML loaded, so missing keys may not actually fall back to `SiteSetting.default_locale` or `:en`.

Translation cache key omits fallback order/default locale

After this change, the result of a cached translation can depend on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (and the hardcoded `:en` fallback), but the cache key is only key + current locale + backend object id. If the default locale changes and `I18n.reload!` is not called, cached missing-key translations will continue to return the old fallback language. Include the fallback chain/default locale in the cache key or ensure invalidation on fallback changes.

Unconditional call to custom `ensure_loaded!` can raise

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` assumes the fallbacks object is the custom `FallbackLocaleList`. If another initializer, plugin, or test replaces `I18n.fallbacks` with a standard fallback object, every request will raise NoMethodError. Consider calling it only when `I18n.fallbacks.respond_to?(:ensure_loaded!)`.

Fallback list ignores hash storage and assignments

`FallbackLocaleList` subclasses Hash but overrides `[]` to always recompute the chain and never consult stored entries. Normal fallback customization such as `I18n.fallbacks[:zh_TW] = [:zh_CN, :en]` will silently have no effect. If fallbacks are intended to be extensible, the class should merge stored/custom entries or expose an explicit extension point.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

Plugin request logs no longer include traceID

The previous LoggerMiddleware explicitly appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext` to the log parameters. This change removes that field, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only adds endpoint, plugin ID, data source, and user fields. Unless an earlier middleware independently injects traceID into the contextual logger, plugin request log lines will no longer contain traceID, weakening trace correlation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

TestLogger.FromContext discards logs and context

TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of a logger that shares the receiver's recorded log state or carries contextual attributes. Because LoggerMiddleware now logs via `logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, tests injecting TestLogger will not observe emitted log records on the original fake, and contextual fields added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware cannot be verified. The fake should return a child/logger that records into the same state or preserves context.

The candidate's additional context concern does not change the matching underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
MetricsMiddleware is a shared mutable middleware instance

The embed layout outputs `parent.postMessage(..., '<%= request.referer %>')`. The Referer header is controlled by the embedding page and is not escaped for JavaScript. A crafted referer can break the script context or potentially inject JavaScript into the Discourse origin, and it also controls the postMessage target origin. false_positives.candidate:
URL scheme validation uses line-start anchor instead of string-start anchor

`return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` uses `^`, which in Ruby matches the beginning of any line. A multiline string containing a non-http scheme followed by a newline and an http URL can pass this check. Use `\A` (and preferably validate the whole URL) to enforce the scheme.

`TopicEmbed.import` immediately mutates its `contents` argument with `contents << ...`. If a caller passes nil (possible from feed/readability extraction) or a frozen string, the import raises instead of failing cleanly. Validate or normalize the content before appending.

The new `cook` path returns `raw` unchanged when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Imported external HTML is untrusted, and the embed view renders `post.cooked` with `raw`. Without sanitization this enables stored XSS from feeds or retrieved embed pages.

`import_remote` opens the URL before validating scheme or safely restricting it

`TopicEmbed.import_remote` calls `open(url).read` before `TopicEmbed.import` applies its http/https check, and `TopicRetriever` only compares the URI host to `embeddable_host`. A URL with a matching host but non-HTTP scheme can reach `open`, allowing unintended fetches or local file access if an open-uri handler supports it. Validate scheme and URL format before opening.

Post side effects are enqueued before the outer embed transaction commits

Inside `Topic.transaction`, `PostCreator#create` runs and enqueues jobs/publishes messages after its own inner transaction but before the surrounding `TopicEmbed` transaction commits. If `TopicEmbed.create!` later fails and the outer transaction rolls back, asynchronous work remains queued for records that were not persisted.

Check-then-create embed can raise unique-index errors under concurrency

`import` checks for an existing `TopicEmbed` and then creates one, while the database has a unique index on `embed_url`. Concurrent first imports of the same URL can both pass the check; one will raise `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`. Rescue the unique violation and reload/use the existing record.

Redis throttle key is set and expired non-atomically

`$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` followed by `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` is not atomic. If the process crashes between the two calls, the key can remain without TTL and permanently throttle retrieval for that embed URL. Use an atomic SET with NX and expiration.

Embed content SHA is updated even if the revision fails

After `PostRevisor#revise!`, `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` runs unconditionally. If the post cannot be revised or saved, the stored SHA no longer matches the post content, causing future content changes to be skipped. Check the revision result before updating the SHA.

`absolutize_urls` can raise on borderline URLs

`URI(url)` is called without rescuing `URI::InvalidURIError`. The preceding URL check only requires an http(s) prefix, so strings with spaces or other invalid characters can reach this method and crash import/retrieval jobs. Validate or rescue invalid URLs and skip them.

`force: true` will drop an existing topic_embeds table

The migration creates `topic_embeds` with `force: true`, which drops the table first. If the table already exists from a prior installation or branch, existing embed mappings are destroyed. Avoid `force: true` in migrations that may run against existing data.

Adding `force: true` to the top_topics migration can drop data

Changing `create_table :top_topics` to use `force: true` makes the migration drop and recreate the table if rerun. This can silently delete existing `top_topics` data. Migrations should not destructively recreate tables that may already contain production data.

Script throws if `discourse-comments` element is absent

`document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` may return null on pages that include `embed.js` but do not have the expected container. The subsequent `comments.appendChild(iframe)` throws and prevents the embed from loading. Guard against the missing element.

Sync path returns a fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific response objects

When sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT; otherwise it returns the provider refresh function's result. Callers are written for the provider result: Google expects res.data, HubSpot expects a token object with accessToken/expiresIn, and Zoho Bigin/CRM expect Axios responses with .data. With sync enabled these callers read undefined properties, throw, or save invalid credentials. The sync response must be normalized to the shape expected by each app.

false_positives.candidate:
prisma is used but not imported

The added credential update calls prisma.credential.update, but the file does not import prisma from @calcom/prisma. This will fail type checking or throw a ReferenceError at runtime when the Salesforce calendar service attempts to refresh credentials.

Zoom refresh uses wrong app slug

The sync helper is called with appSlug 'zoomvideo', but the Zoom app credential is stored/identified by the slug 'zoom' (for example, the OAuth callback creates appId 'zoom'). The external sync endpoint will receive an unrecognized app slug and may return the wrong token or fail. Use 'zoom'.

Updating synced credential does not clear invalid flag

The webhook update path only updates key. If the existing credential has invalid: true from a previous failed refresh, the newly synced valid key remains marked invalid and may be skipped by adapters. The update should also set invalid: false when accepting new synced credentials.

Find-then-create/update credential is not atomic

The endpoint performs findFirst followed by create/update without a transaction or unique-constraint upsert. Concurrent webhook calls for the same user/app can both miss an existing credential and create duplicate credentials, or overwrite each other in an undefined order. This can cause stale or ambiguous OAuth credentials. Use atomic updateMany/create or a transaction with proper uniqueness.

Outbound credential sync request has no authentication or HTTPS enforcement

The outbound request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug and does not include a shared secret, signature, or client authentication. It also does not require HTTPS. If the endpoint is reachable outside a trusted internal network, it can be abused to obtain user tokens, and token responses may be exposed in transit. Add authentication/signing and enforce HTTPS.

Webhook handler accepts all HTTP methods

The handler does not check req.method. A GET or other non-POST request will still execute the webhook logic and likely throw during body parsing, returning a 500 instead of a 405. Restrict the route to POST.

Salesforce client refreshes token unconditionally

getClient always calls the Salesforce OAuth token endpoint before creating a connection, even if the stored access token has not expired. This creates unnecessary refresh requests and can cause rate limiting or latency. Check the token expiry and refresh only when needed.

No automated tests for credential sync webhook

This adds a security-sensitive webhook that can create/replace OAuth credentials and changes token refresh flows across many apps, but no automated tests are included for authentication, encryption/decryption, invalid payloads, duplicate handling, or sync-enabled refresh behavior. Without tests these regressions are easy to reintroduce.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Workflow reminder cancellations are not awaited when cancelling bookings

In handleCancelBooking, deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called inside forEach loops without collecting or awaiting their promises. The handler then continues and returns. In Next.js/serverless execution the process may be frozen after the response, so the database update marking email reminders as cancelled or the SMS cancellation may never complete. This can leave reminders active for cancelled bookings and cause emails/SMS to still be sent.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without awaiting their promises inside forEach loops, potentially leaving reminders active. It focuses on booking cancellation, which is one of the affected flows described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete cancels SendGrid but does not delete or mark the reminder record

deleteScheduledEmailReminder's immediateDelete branch cancels the SendGrid scheduled send but returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row or setting cancelled=true. Only callers that immediately cascade-delete the reminder can tolerate this, and even there the call is not awaited. For callers such as rescheduling, this leaves stale scheduled reminder rows and removes any ability to retry a failed cancellation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the immediateDelete branch cancels the SendGrid send but leaves the WorkflowReminder database record undeleted and not marked cancelled, causing stale or orphaned records. The candidate does not mention the omitted SendGrid DELETE API call, but it matches the central underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Paid booking cancellation path skips workflow reminder cancellation

When bookingToDelete.paid is true, handleCancelBooking refunds the payment and returns before reaching the code that cancels scheduled jobs and workflow reminders. As a result, paid bookings that are rejected/cancelled do not have their workflow reminders cancelled, so reminder emails or SMS can still be sent for these bookings.

Cron cancellation query does not restrict to valid scheduled email reminders

The remindersToCancel query selects all WorkflowReminder rows with cancelled=true but does not filter by method=EMAIL, scheduled=true, or referenceId non-null. The code then posts reminder.referenceId to SendGrid as batch_id. Any SMS reminder or email reminder with a null referenceId in this state will cause an invalid SendGrid request, which can abort the cancellation loop for all reminders.

One failed cancellation aborts processing of all remaining cancelled reminders

The SendGrid cancellation loop is wrapped in a single try/catch. If any one client.request or delete fails, execution jumps to the catch block and the remaining cancelled reminders are neither cancelled in SendGrid nor deleted from the database. The endpoint then continues and may return success. A single bad or stale reminder can therefore block cancellation of all cancelled workflow emails on every cron run.

Unscheduled reminder query does not exclude cancelled reminders

The unscheduledReminders query filters only on method=EMAIL and scheduled=false; it does not exclude rows where cancelled=true. If a reminder ever reaches this state due to a race condition, manual data correction, or future code change, the cron will schedule and send an email for a cancelled booking. The query should exclude cancelled=true rows.

Deferred cancellation can still send imminent reminders

For non-immediate cancellations, deleteScheduledEmailReminder only sets cancelled=true, while the cron job cancels SendGrid emails only when the scheduled date is within the next hour and runs every 15 minutes. If a booking is cancelled shortly before a reminder is due, for example a few minutes before sending, the reminder may be sent before the cron job performs the SendGrid cancellation. Near-term reminders should be cancelled synchronously or immediately.

requestReschedule does not await reminder cancellation

In the requestReschedule mutation, deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called inside a forEach loop without awaiting the promises. The mutation can return before the email reminders are marked cancelled or SMS cancellations complete, so old reminders for a rescheduled booking may still be sent.

Workflow deletion cancels external scheduled messages without awaiting them

When deleting a workflow, scheduled reminders are cancelled with async deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder calls inside forEach, and then the workflow is deleted without awaiting those operations. Because deleting the workflow cascades to reminder rows, if the external SendGrid/Twilio cancellation does not finish or fails, no database record remains to retry and the scheduled email/SMS may still be sent.

Workflow update mutation does not await async step processing

In the workflow update mutation, userWorkflow.steps.map(async ...) performs step deletion/update, reminder cancellation, and reminder creation, but the returned promises are not awaited. The mutation can return before these operations complete, leaving workflow steps, active event types, or reminders in an inconsistent state, especially in serverless environments.

Failed SMS cancellation leaves reminder active with no retry

deleteScheduledSMSReminder calls twilio.cancelSMS and only deletes the WorkflowReminder if that call succeeds. If the Twilio request throws, the error is swallowed and the reminder row remains scheduled. There is no cancelled state or retry mechanism for SMS reminders, so a transient provider failure can result in an SMS reminder still being sent for a cancelled or rescheduled booking.

false_positives.candidate:
Read-then-create attendee update can create duplicates under concurrent requests

The handler reads existing attendees, filters guests, then creates attendees without a transaction, upsert, or guaranteed unique constraint. Two simultaneous addGuests calls with the same email can both pass the filter and create duplicate attendee rows, or cause unhandled database errors if a constraint exists.

Calendar update uses caller credentials instead of booking owner credentials

EventManager is constructed with ctx.user and credentials from getUsersCredentials(ctx.user), even when the caller is only an attendee or team admin. The handler fetches booking.user.credentials but never uses them, so calendar updates may fail or target the caller's calendar rather than the booking owner's destination calendar.

Guests can be added to cancelled or past bookings via API

After loading the booking, the handler does not check booking.status or whether the event has ended before inserting attendees, updating calendars, and sending emails. An authenticated organizer/attendee can call addGuests for cancelled or past bookings, causing inappropriate notifications and calendar updates.

No maximum limit on guests array

The guests field is an unbounded array of emails. An authenticated user could submit a very large list, causing bulk attendee creation, mass email sending, and calendar API load. Add a reasonable maximum array length.

Seated event types are not handled when adding guests

For event types using seatsPerTimeSlot, the handler creates plain attendee rows without checking remaining seats or creating seat references. This can exceed seat capacity and leave seated bookings in an inconsistent state.

Organizer lookup throws for bookings without a userId

The organizer lookup uses prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow with id: booking.userId || 0. If a booking can have a null userId, such as some team bookings, this queries user id 0 and throws, causing a 500 instead of handling the team/userPrimaryEmail case.

Error toast always prefixes undefined and never falls back

onError builds a message string from err.data?.code and err.message, then uses message || t('unable_to_add_guests'). When err.data?.code is absent, the message becomes 'undefined: ...' and is truthy, so the fallback is never shown. Build the message conditionally and provide a proper fallback.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

After decrypting `user.backupCodes`, the code sets the used entry to null and writes the whole encrypted array back. Two parallel successful logins can read the same array before either update completes; one update can overwrite the other, restoring an already-used code, or the same code can be accepted by both requests. One-time backup codes are therefore not guaranteed to be single-use. Use a transaction/row lock or an atomic consumption mechanism.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

Blob object URL for backup-code download is not revoked on close/unmount

`URL.createObjectURL` is called during setup, but the URL is only revoked if setup runs again. Closing the modal or unmounting the component leaves the blob URL alive, causing a small memory leak. Revoke the URL in a cleanup effect or when the modal closes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: the backup-code blob object URL is not revoked when the component unmounts, potentially causing a memory leak. The candidate additionally mentions modal closure and a cleanup fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code sign-in can bypass password/first-factor verification

In the CredentialsProvider authorize function, the password is verified only when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The backup-code path at line 131 is taken whenever `credentials.backupCode` is present. A caller can therefore POST credentials containing a valid `backupCode` and an arbitrary non-empty `totpCode`; the password check is skipped and the backup code alone authenticates the user. For password accounts this removes the password factor, and for non-CAL identity-provider accounts it also bypasses the OAuth/SAML first factor. Consequence: account takeover if a backup code is known or leaked.

Modal state reset does not clear react-hook-form/TOTP value

`resetState` only clears password, error, and step; it does not call `form.reset()` or clear the registered `totpCode`. Because the component auto-submits when `totpCode?.trim().length === 6` (line 157), a stale six-digit value left from a previous enable attempt can trigger an unintended enable request or surface errors when the modal is reopened. It also leaves secret/backup-code state and object URLs in memory.

2FA enable success is not propagated if backup-code dialog is dismissed

After `handleEnable` succeeds, the modal moves to the backup-code step and calls `onEnable` only from the explicit Close button. If the user closes the dialog with Escape/overlay/close affordance, `onOpenChange` closes the modal without calling `onEnable`, even though 2FA has already been enabled server-side. The settings UI can remain in the disabled/stale state until a refresh.

No e2e coverage for the new backup-code login/disable paths

The PR adds UI for backup codes and server-side consumption, but the tests only verify that the codes are displayed/copied/downloaded. The TODO acknowledges missing tests for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code. Without coverage, the critical backup-code authentication/consumption logic can regress unnoticed.

Password visibility toggle is removed from keyboard focus

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button prevents keyboard users from focusing and activating it. This makes the password field less accessible; the control should remain focusable or provide an equivalent keyboard-accessible alternative.

Backup code input is assumed to be a string

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` is called without validating the body field type. A malformed POST with a number/object/array for `backupCode` will throw a TypeError and return a 500 instead of a validation error. Validate/sanitize the field as a string before processing; the same assumption exists in the NextAuth credentials handler.

Submitting an empty backup-code form can fail silently

The login form has `noValidate`, so the BackupCode input's required/minLength attributes are not enforced. If a user is on the lost-access screen and submits an empty backup code, the server falls back to the TOTP branch and returns `second-factor-required`; the client merely keeps the two-factor screen and displays no error, leaving the user stuck. Show an error or validate the backup code client-side before submitting.

If such a provider is discovered but ignored because another provider has equal or higher order, those global side effects remain even though the provider is not the selected CryptoProvider.

DER-to-raw ECDSA conversion silently truncates oversized integers

integerToBytes copies the last qLength bytes when the encoded integer is longer than qLength. This silently truncates oversized R/S values instead of rejecting them. DER-to-raw ECDSA signature conversion should only strip a single leading zero byte and should reject values that do not fit in the expected fixed length; otherwise malformed signatures are transformed into incorrect raw values instead of causing a validation error.

The test generates one default EC key pair and uses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. JOSE ES256/ES384/ES512 require P-256, P-384 and P-521 respectively, with different signature lengths. The test also does not verify the converted DER signature with Signature.verify, so it cannot detect semantically invalid conversions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator uses unsupported negative QuerySet slicing

When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset is negative, the code sets start_offset to the negative offset and executes queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices, so this raises an AssertionError rather than performing efficient reverse pagination. Because cursor offsets are parsed from client input, a crafted cursor can trigger a 500 on endpoints using this paginator. Negative offsets should be rejected or handled without negative QuerySet slices.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator slices a Django queryset with negative offsets. Django does not support negative slicing, so this raises an AssertionError.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate AuditLogEntry.datetime

The endpoint selects OptimizedCursorPaginator while ordering by -datetime. Unlike DateTimePaginator, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil directly on the field value and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime. AuditLogEntry.datetime is a datetime, so the first non-empty optimized page raises TypeError when build_cursor computes a key, and any non-zero cursor would also filter a datetime column with a numeric value. This makes the optimized pagination path fail with 500 or invalid queries. Use DateTimePaginator or make OptimizedCursorPaginator handle datetime conversion.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to the datetime field when ordering by -datetime, which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:

The new start_offset calculation uses cursor.offset unchanged when cursor.is_prev is true. Cursor.from_string accepts negative integers, so a cursor like 0:-1:1 causes queryset[-1:stop], which Django QuerySets do not support, leading to a 500 on any BasePaginator-derived endpoint. For non-prev cursors, negative offsets are silently coerced to 0, which can mask malformed input and return the wrong page. Cursor offsets should be validated as non-negative.

Extra-row drop condition compares against an impossible length

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, after slicing from start_offset, results can contain at most limit + extra rows, but the code checks len(results) == offset + limit + extra. When cursor.offset is greater than zero, this condition cannot be true, so the extra row fetched for backward pagination may not be removed. This can return one too many rows or produce incorrect prev-cursor state. The check should compare against the number of rows actually requested, e.g. limit + extra or stop - start_offset.

Typo order_b prevents changing queryset ordering

The intended ordering change is silently lost, so previous-page pagination can query in the wrong order and return incorrect results. This affects BasePaginator and its subclasses used by the new optimized path.

The PR introduces a query-parameter-controlled paginator switch and a new paginator with cursor, datetime, and negative-offset behavior, but no tests. At minimum, tests are needed for the optimized audit-log endpoint covering empty and non-empty pages, next and prev cursors, malformed or negative offsets, and permission fallback when optimized_pagination is absent or the user lacks access. Without tests, these failure modes are easy to regress.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

This can create duplicate memory indexes, concurrently open or write the same file-based directory, and overwrite the cache entry, causing wasted work, leaks, or corrupted indexes. true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while BuildIndex writes to it concurrently, which risks a concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate leaves out the specific call site (the event watcher goroutine), but the underlying bug is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared variables are written concurrently in search init

In searchSupport.init, each errgroup goroutine assigns to the outer err variable and increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. This is a data race: the stored error and counter are nondeterministic, and race-detector runs will fail. Use a local error per goroutine and an atomic counter or channel.

Initial index build can miss writes that occur while building

searchSupport.init builds indexes first and discards the resource version returned by build, then calls WatchWriteEvents after all builds are complete. The watch starts from the latest resource version at that later time, so writes that happen during the potentially long initial build are not applied to the new indexes. This can leave search results stale until affected resources are written again. Start watching before building or backfill events from the RV returned by build.

Watch event goroutine does not handle a closed events channel

The goroutine in searchSupport.init receives from events with a single-value receive and ignores whether the channel is closed. If the storage backend closes the channel, the loop receives nil events forever and handleEvent will dereference a nil *WrittenEvent, causing a panic or tight loop. Use v, ok := <-events and return when !ok, and select on a cancellable context.

Search watcher is started with an uncancellable background context

searchSupport.init creates watchctx := context.Background() and starts an event-processing goroutine with no way to stop it. server.Stop cancels the server context but does not cancel this context, so the goroutine can leak, especially in tests or when resource servers are recreated. Use a cancellable context tied to the server lifecycle.

IndexMetrics is used without nil checks in event handling

handleEvent updates IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds for ADDED and DELETED events without checking whether IndexMetrics is nil, while other code paths in the same file guard with if IndexMetrics != nil. If metrics are not initialized, the first watch event will panic. Add nil checks or ensure metrics are always initialized.

History and Origin can panic when search is not configured

server.History and server.Origin call s.search.History and s.search.Origin without checking whether s.search is nil. server.Search performs this check, but History and Origin do not. If the resource server is created without search support and these gRPC methods are called, the server will panic. Return a not-configured error when s.search is nil.

Update swallows backend read errors

In server.Update, if s.backend.ReadResource returns a response with Error set, the method returns an empty UpdateResponse and a nil error without setting rsp.Error. Clients cannot distinguish a backend failure from a successful response with no data. Propagate the backend error in rsp.Error or return an error.

Constructor does not clean up when Init fails

NewResourceServer creates a cancelable context and may initialize lifecycle/search state, but if s.Init fails it returns without calling cancel or stopping lifecycle hooks. This can leak goroutines or backend resources during failed startups or in tests. Call cancel and appropriate cleanup before returning the error.

Replacing a cache entry does not close the previous index

BuildIndex assigns the newly built bleveIndex into b.cache without closing any existing index for the same key. If a rebuild or a concurrent build race replaces an entry, the old bleve.Index remains open, leaking memory/file handles and possibly retaining locks on file-based indexes. Close or remove old indexes when replacing cache entries.

Poller span is not ended when listLatestRVs fails

In backend.poller, a span is started for each poll tick. If b.listLatestRVs returns an error, the code logs and continues without calling span.End(), leaking tracing state. End the span before continuing, for example with defer or an explicit span.End().

GetResourceStats creates a span with tracePrefix + '.GetResourceStats' while tracePrefix already ends with a dot, producing 'sql.resource..GetResourceStats'. Use tracePrefix + 'GetResourceStats' or adjust the prefix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Several tests pass arguments that do not match the evaluated packet, such as building an expected occurrence with value 6 for a group whose packet value is 10, or building an occurrence for one group key while evaluating another. false_positives.candidate:
get_state_data raises KeyError when a stateful detector has no counters

In StatefulDetectorHandler.get_state_data, counter_updates is initialized to {} and only populated if self.counter_names is truthy. The later construction of DetectorStateData unconditionally accesses counter_updates[gk]. If a subclass defines counter_names as an empty list, any call with non-empty group_keys raises KeyError. Initialize counter_updates to {gk: {} for gk in group_keys} or handle the no-counter case explicitly.

Redis state keys collide for None and empty-string group keys

build_dedupe_value_key, and similarly build_counter_value_key, converts a None group_key to an empty string before formatting the Redis key. A real group_key of '' therefore produces the same Redis key as None. Since DetectorState rows and fingerprints can distinguish None from '', dedupe values and counters can be shared or overwritten between these two group keys, causing skipped evaluations or wrong detector state. Use a distinct sentinel for None or otherwise namespace the keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.

false_positives.candidate:
Incident can be created before failure_issue_threshold failures when history is short

When failure_issue_threshold > 1, the code slices the last `failure_issue_threshold` check-ins and only checks whether any of them is OK. It never verifies that `len(previous_checkins) >= failure_issue_threshold`. For a monitor environment with fewer check-ins than the threshold and no OK check-in (for example, a new monitor whose first check-ins fail), the function proceeds to set MonitorStatus.ERROR and create a MonitorIncident, effectively treating the threshold as 1. This can create incidents earlier than configured.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

The dataclass default is written as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`, so `timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the module is imported. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value, including via `from_dict` when `queued` is missing, will carry that same stale timestamp instead of the time the assignment change was queued. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once, when the class is defined or the module is imported, so every instance shares one stale timestamp.

false_positives.candidate:
from_dict silently discards invalid or unknown serialized payloads

`AssignmentSource.from_dict` constructs the dataclass with `cls(**input_dict)` and returns `None` on `TypeError`/`ValueError`. Any unexpected extra key in the serialized payload causes the entire assignment source to be dropped, and the dataclass constructor does not validate or coerce types; for example, `integration_id` may remain a string and `queued` is not parsed back into a datetime after JSON round-trips. In `sync_assignee_outbound`, a dropped or invalid source is treated as no source, which can allow an outbound sync back to the integration that originated the change and defeat the cycle prevention. Validate required fields, coerce types, and tolerate unknown fields or log failures instead of silently returning `None`.

No test that deassign with a matching AssignmentSource suppresses outbound sync

The PR adds cycle prevention to both `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` and `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign`, but the new matching-source test only covers assignment. The existing unassign test calls `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(self.group)` without an assignment source and asserts outbound sync happens; there is no test that deassigning with `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` does not call `sync_assignee_outbound` for the same integration. A regression in the deassign path could reintroduce sync loops without being caught.

Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Factory-owned queue pool is shut down by strategy close

ResultsStrategyFactory creates a single FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes it to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() shuts that pool down. Arroyo recreates processing strategies on partition rebalances, so closing the old strategy permanently stops the shared workers/queues; the next strategy created for the new assignment will submit work to a shut-down pool and messages may be dropped or rejected. The pool lifecycle must be owned by the factory, or a new pool must be created per strategy.

OffsetTracker iterates all_offsets while other threads can add partitions

get_committable_offsets builds `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` without a lock protecting the key set. add_offset can insert a new partition key concurrently under a per-partition lock. In CPython this can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`, causing the commit loop to fail and potentially delaying or interrupting offset commits whenever new partitions appear.

OffsetTracker can commit past untracked offset gaps

get_committable_offsets uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. If the offset immediately after `last_committed` was never added to `all_offsets` (for example, a message skipped because it was not a BrokerValue, filtered before submit, or lost due to an error), `min_offset` jumps past that gap and later completed offsets become committable. This can commit past an unseen offset and violates the intended contiguous-offset commit guarantee.

Workers exit instead of draining queues during shutdown

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets `worker.shutdown = True` and then calls `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`. OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on `while not self.shutdown`; if shutdown is set while items remain in the queue, the worker exits after finishing its current item and leaves the rest of the queued work unprocessed. This defeats graceful draining on shutdown.

join()/close() stop committing before draining in-flight work

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout and calls close(). close() sets the shutdown event, joins the commit thread, and then shuts down the pool. It does not wait for queues to become empty or perform a final commit after workers drain. During graceful shutdown, queued or in-flight items may be left unprocessed or processed after commits stop, so their offsets are not committed.

Unbounded queues and no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll only emits metrics. If workers fall behind, the consumer thread can continue consuming Kafka messages and enqueueing them without bound, causing memory growth. The PR description mentions natural backpressure, but no backpressure mechanism is implemented.

Failed work items are marked complete and can be committed

OrderedQueueWorker catches exceptions from result processing and then calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset` in the finally block. ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows exceptions. A message that fails processing is therefore treated as done and may be committed, dropping the result with no retry or DLQ. Transient failures can cause silent data loss.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and workers catch `queue.ShutDown`. These APIs were added in Python 3.13. On older supported interpreters shutdown raises AttributeError (caught and logged), workers may remain blocked in `get()`, and exception matching on `queue.ShutDown` can fail. Graceful shutdown will be unreliable unless Python >= 3.13 is required.

Commit callback is invoked from a background thread

_commit_loop calls the Arroyo commit callback from a dedicated daemon thread. The commit callback/commit policy is normally driven by the stream processor thread, and there is no synchronization here with poll/close/join or partition rebalances. If the callback or underlying consumer state is not thread-safe, this can race and corrupt commit state or cause commits during shutdown/rebalance.

decode_payload asserts on FilteredPayload in queue mode

ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload asserts that the payload is not FilteredPayload, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy expects a decoder to return None for filtered/invalid messages. In thread-queue mode a FilteredPayload triggers AssertionError, which is caught by the strategy's generic error path and logged as an unexpected submit error before being marked complete. Filtered payloads should be handled explicitly by returning None.

Negative max_workers creates an invalid queue pool

FixedQueuePool is created with `num_queues=max_workers or 20`. This handles None and 0 but not negative values. A negative `--max-workers` would create no queues and later queue selection/submission would fail or behave unpredictably. max_workers should be validated to be positive.

Error-handling test asserts behavior the implementation does not guarantee

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling makes processing raise and asserts that no offsets are committed. The implementation marks failed work items complete and may commit them after the commit loop's one-second interval, so the test only passes if it finishes before that commit. It is timing-dependent and validates the wrong behavior; it should deterministically assert the intended failure semantics.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator will crash

When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset is negative, OptimizedCursorPaginator slices the queryset with a negative start offset and possibly a negative stop offset. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing, so this raises AssertionError. Since cursor offsets come from client-provided cursor strings and the audit-log endpoint enables advanced features, an authorized user can trigger a 500.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator passing a negative cursor.offset as the queryset slice start when advanced features are enabled. Django does not support negative queryset indexing.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now passes negative prev offsets to QuerySet slicing

The new start_offset logic uses cursor.offset directly when cursor.is_prev is true. If a client supplies a negative offset in a previous-page cursor, the queryset is sliced with a negative offset. Django QuerySets do not support negative offsets, so this raises AssertionError. This affects all BasePaginator subclasses, including DateTimePaginator.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. In BasePaginator, when cursor.is_prev is true, start_offset is set to the offset without clamping, so a negative offset is passed to queryset slicing.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optimized paginator is incompatible with datetime ordering

The endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by='-datetime'. OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on the field value and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value, while AuditLogEntry.datetime is a datetime. Any non-empty optimized page will raise TypeError, and the cursor value would also be compared to a timestamp column as an integer.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate names the same bug as the golden comment. OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime key under order_by='-datetime', which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Typo prevents reversing queryset ordering for previous pages

In BasePaginator.build_queryset, when converting an existing '-key' ordering to ascending for a previous page, the code assigns to queryset.query.order_b instead of queryset.query.order_by. The queryset ordering is therefore not changed, so previous-page pagination can query with the wrong ORDER BY and return incorrect results. This affects paginators built on BasePaginator, including the new OptimizedCursorPaginator.

Changing span-buf:s:* keys from sets to sorted sets is not migration-safe

The PR changes span buffer keys from Redis sets (SADD/SCARD/SSCAN) to sorted sets (ZADD/ZCARD/ZSCAN) while keeping the same key names. Existing in-flight keys written by the old code can remain for up to redis_ttl, default 3600 seconds. New ZADD/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN operations on those set-typed keys will return WRONGTYPE errors, causing span buffering and flushing failures during rollout.

Silent eviction can drop spans, including root spans, and ignores configured limits

The Lua script uses ZPOPMIN to remove the lowest-scored members whenever a segment has more than 1000 spans. This silently discards spans, can evict the root/segment span while leaving the has_root_span flag set, and bypasses the Python max_segment_spans configuration. There is no metric or log, so incomplete segments can be produced without observability.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM can corrupt span scores

The Lua script uses ZUNIONSTORE without specifying AGGREGATE. If the same span payload/member exists in both source sorted sets, Redis sums the end_timestamp_precise scores. The corrupted score changes eviction order and can prevent the span from being evicted when expected. An explicit AGGREGATE MAX or MIN should be used.

max_segment_spans parameter is now ignored

SpansBuffer still accepts and stores max_segment_spans, but the new Lua script hardcodes the cap at 1000 and the Python flush path no longer enforces max_segment_spans. Callers configuring this parameter will get a different silent limit and a behavior change from skipping oversized segments to evicting spans.

Consumer assumes end_timestamp_precise is present and valid

process_batch indexes val['end_timestamp_precise'] and passes it directly to Redis ZADD as a score. If a message lacks the field, has null, or has a non-numeric value, the consumer raises KeyError/TypeError and processing stops. Since this field is newly required by the buffer, invalid or older messages need validation or a safe fallback.

Redirect-chain limit reduced to 1000 may split deep traces

The redirect resolution loop was lowered from 10000 to 1000. If a redirect chain is longer than 1000, the script stops early and maps the span to an intermediate set, which can prevent related spans from being merged into the same segment. This trades correctness for bounded runtime and should be documented or metered.

No tests cover eviction, large segments, or sorted-set migration

The updated tests only add end_timestamp_precise to small segments. They do not create more than 1000 spans, do not verify which spans are evicted by score, do not test duplicate-member ZUNIONSTORE behavior, and do not cover interaction with old set-typed keys. Given the new data-dropping behavior, this is a significant test gap.

Optimized audit-log pagination path has no tests

The new optimized_pagination branch and OptimizedCursorPaginator are not covered by tests. Given the datetime incompatibility and negative-offset crash paths, this endpoint/paginator combination needs explicit tests before merging.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the original dataset/request instead of the query actually executed

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset`, and may later execute a modified query such as a dashboard-split query (`... AND !event.type:transaction` or `... AND event.type:transaction`). However the upsampling eligibility check is computed from the outer `dataset` and the original HTTP request only: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. It does not consider the actual `scoped_dataset` or the final `query` being executed. This can cause the `count()` rewrite to be applied to a transaction-like query, or skipped for an error-only split query, leading to incorrect counts or query failures. The eligibility check should be based on the actual dataset and query passed to the query executor.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset. Both cite dashboard split paths, where this can cause upsampling to be skipped incorrectly.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental submodule/gitlink added to repository root

The PR adds a file named `sentry-repo` containing a Git subproject commit pointer. This looks like an accidental embedded repository/submodule rather than an intentional source change. There is no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry or documented reason for it, and it can break clones, CI checkouts, and tooling that does not expect an embedded repository at the repo root. It should be removed from the PR.

Substring check for `event.type:error` can misclassify discover queries

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`. This is unsafe for Sentry search syntax: it matches negated queries such as `!event.type:error`, compound queries such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and text inside quoted values. For the discover dataset this enables `upsampled_count()` for mixed or non-error event queries, where `sample_weight` may be missing, zero, or inapplicable, producing silently incorrect counts. The check needs to parse/understand the query rather than using a raw substring match.

`upsampled_count` assumes valid integral `sample_weight` values

The new `upsampled_count` aggregate is implemented as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. This has two data-correctness risks: (1) if any event in an allowlisted project has a NULL/missing/zero `sample_weight`, the contribution can be dropped or become zero even though the event exists; (2) if `sample_weight` can be fractional, `toInt64` truncates the summed result and biases counts downward. Project-level allowlisting does not by itself guarantee every event has a valid integral weight. Consider using an explicit fallback such as `coalesce(sample_weight, 1)` and avoiding lossy integer casting unless weights are guaranteed integral.

Eligibility cache can serve stale upsampling decisions and invalidation is not wired

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches project allowlist eligibility for 60 seconds keyed by organization and project set. If the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes during that window, especially when a project is removed from the allowlist, queries can continue to use upsampled counts incorrectly. The provided `invalidate_upsampling_cache` helper is not called from anywhere, and it only invalidates one exact project-set key rather than all affected keys. This creates a data-integrity window after configuration changes. Include a config/version token in the cache key or wire up broader invalidation.

Cache key construction sorts and hashes all project IDs on every call

The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))` before checking whether the dataset/query is even eligible for upsampling. For organizations with many projects, this adds sorting and hashing overhead to every events-stats request, including datasets where upsampling is never applied. A cheaper early-out for non-applicable datasets, or a more efficient stable key, would avoid undermining the stated performance optimization.

Endpoint tests do not exercise the explicit `errors` dataset path

The upsampling helper unconditionally applies for the `errors` dataset, but the added endpoint tests only use the default/discover path and one explicit `dataset=discover` case. There is no test with `dataset=errors`, so the branch where the rewrite is always enabled for the errors dataset is not covered. This is important because the new SnQL function was added in the discover dataset configuration and the errors-dataset behavior may differ.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cache key can collide because fields are joined with underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with underscores and no escaping. Grafana resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different name/parent pairs can produce the same key, for example name a_b with parent c and name a with parent b_c. A denial cached for one combination can then incorrectly deny another resource. Use an unambiguous encoding, hash, or separator that cannot appear in UIDs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug. userPermDenialCacheKey joins its fields with underscores and no escaping, so different inputs can produce the same key and cause incorrect denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type

Check builds the denial-cache key from namespace, UserUID, action, name, and parent folder, but not IdentityType. Anonymous and renderer identities can both have UID 0, and user/service account UIDs may also overlap or be supplied in different forms. A denial cached for one identity type can therefore be returned for another identity type, skipping its permission lookup and causing incorrect access denials. Include the identity type in the denial cache key.

Denial cache is checked before positive permissions and never invalidated

The denial cache is consulted before any positive cached or database permissions and is only cleared by TTL. If a check is denied while permissions are being created or replicated, the denial entry remains and blocks subsequent checks even after the permission exists. This can keep a creator from accessing a newly created dashboard or folder for the TTL, which conflicts with the stated goal of the PR. Consider checking positive permissions before the denial cache, deleting denial entries when a fresh check allows, or not negative-caching checks for resources that may be in the process of being created.

Unauthorized checks can force repeated database permission queries

Check now falls back to getIdentityPermissions whenever the cached permission set does not explicitly allow the requested resource, even if the permission cache was just populated. Sequential checks for many distinct unauthorized resources will each trigger a full database permission query before their negative cache entry is written. This can substantially increase database load and can be amplified by authenticated enumeration. Consider limiting requeries, using cache age, or keeping cached-permission denials for non-existent resources.

Error-path test does not actually test an error

The test case named should return error if store fails does not set fakeStore.err and the test asserts require.NoError, so it never exercises the error path. Add an expected error flag and make the fake store fail for this case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Installation crashes if integration metadata lacks sender.login

GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] unconditionally. build_integration only stores metadata.sender when state has a sender, so older integrations, integrations created before the webhook/state was populated, or any installation whose metadata lacks sender will raise KeyError. The result is a 500 instead of the controlled installation-failure page, blocking legitimate installs/reinstalls. Use safe lookup and fail closed when either authenticated user or sender login is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: integration.metadata['sender']['login'] is accessed without checking that the sender key exists, which raises a KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
New user validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist

When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") to the GitHub user who performed the installation. installation_id is still user supplied (request.GET overrides bound state at line 448) and is later used by build_integration to create/attach the integration. If the Sentry Integration row is missing because of webhook delay, deletion, or legacy data, the security check fails open and an OAuth-authenticated user can continue with an arbitrary installation_id. The flow should require a verified sender/installation association or abort when it cannot verify the installer.

Failures while fetching the authenticated GitHub user are unhandled

OAuthLoginView.dispatch catches only exceptions while parsing the access-token response. get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) can raise network errors, HTTP errors, rate-limit errors, or return an unexpected payload. In those cases the request will 500 rather than rendering the intended github-integration-failed error page. Wrap the token exchange/user-info fetch in exception handling and return error(...) for expected failures.

installation_id is inserted into the GitHub API path without validation

installation_id comes from user input/pipeline state and is interpolated directly into /app/installations/{installation_id}. If a non-numeric or path-containing value is supplied, it may request unintended GitHub API paths. Validate that installation_id matches GitHub's numeric installation ID format (or otherwise sanitize/quote it) before making the API call.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup removes literal "alias" instead of the created identity provider aliases

In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup registration uses testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove instead of the actual created alias ("idp-alias-" + i). The same mistake occurs later for idp-alias-20. As a result, the test does not clean up the identity providers it creates and may attempt to remove a nonexistent provider named "alias", leaking realm state or causing cleanup failures.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug. The cleanup uses the literal "alias" instead of "idp-alias-" + i, so the created identity providers are not removed.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update can miss changes because it uses an organization-aware model

update() retrieves the current identity provider via getById(), which returns an organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() also checks whether the linked organization exists and is enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then applies LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate(), whose ENABLED filter calls this overridden isEnabled(). If the linked organization is disabled or missing, the original model is treated as not available for login even though it may still be present in the .idp.login cache. An update that changes hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or BROKER_PUBLIC while the organization is disabled can therefore hit the 'both not login' no-invalidation branch, leaving stale cached login lists. When the organization is enabled again, getForLogin() can return identity providers that should now be hidden, link-only, or not public. The invalidation decision should be based on the raw persisted IDP fields (or the delegate model), not the organization-aware dynamic isEnabled(), and/or organization lifecycle changes should invalidate these login caches.

REALM_ONLY login cache entries are duplicated per organizationId

getForLogin() uses organizationId as the search key for all fetch modes. For FetchMode.REALM_ONLY the organizationId parameter is semantically ignored, so calls with different organization IDs can create separate cached search entries under the same REALM_ONLY cache key containing the same realm-level identity providers. This wastes cache space and can cause unnecessary delegate lookups. For REALM_ONLY, organizationId should be normalized to the empty search key.

Single login cache entry accumulates results for all organization IDs

The login cache is keyed only by realm and FetchMode, while different organizationId values are stored as additional search keys inside the same IdentityProviderListQuery. In realms with many organizations, the ORG_ONLY/ALL cache entry can grow without bound as distinct organization logins occur, and any qualifying identity-provider change invalidates the whole entry. This can create a large cache object and a contention hotspot. Consider per-organization cache keys or another strategy to bound the accumulated search-key state.
